text:
“Our old dean has awakened to new life and new strength,” said a third. “Every Sunday he speaks to us about the coming of the kingdom of God. Who can wish to sin any longer? The reign of goodness is at hand.”

And the major’s wife drove slowly onward, asking whomever she met:

“How are things with you? Are you not suffering want here in the district?”

And the feverish heat and the stabbing pain in her breast subsided when they answered her:

“There are two good, wealthy women here, Marianne Sinclaire and Anna Stjärnhök. They help Gösta Berling go from house to house and make sure that no one need starve. And nowadays no grain is thrown into the brandy still.”

It was as though the major’s wife had sat there in the sleigh and conducted a long church service. She had come to a holy land. She saw old, furrowed faces brighten when people spoke of the times that had come. The sick forgot their pains to praise the day of joy.

“We all want to be like the good Captain Lennart,” they said. “We all want to be good. We want to believe good of everyone. We do not want to harm anyone. Such things will hasten the coming of the kingdom of God.”

She found them all seized by the same spirit. At the manor houses, free meals were provided for those in greatest need. Whoever had work to be done now had it carried out, and at all the major’s wife’s works, activity was in full swing.

Never had she felt healthier than when she sat there and let the cold air stream into her aching breast. She could not pass a single farm without stopping to ask.

“Now all is well,” the household would then say. “Great distress was at hand here, but the good gentlemen from Ekeby are helping us. The major’s wife will be astonished at everything that has been accomplished there. Now the mill is almost finished, and the smithy is in operation, and the burned house has been timbered up to the roof ridge.”

It was the distress and the heart-shaking events that had transformed them all. Ah, surely it would last only a little while! But it was good nevertheless to return to a land where one served another and where everyone wished to do good. The major’s wife felt that she could forgive the cavaliers, and she thanked God for it.

“Anna Lisa,” she said, “I, an old woman, sit here believing that I am already journeying into the heaven of the blessed.”

When she finally arrived at Ekeby and the cavaliers hurried over to help her out of the sleigh, they could scarcely recognize her, for she was as good and gentle as their own young countess. The older ones, who had seen her when she was young, whispered to one another:

“It is not the major’s wife of Ekeby; it is Margareta Celsing returning.”

Great was the cavaliers’ joy at seeing her arrive so good and so free of all thoughts of vengeance, but it soon changed to sorrow when they discovered how ill she was. She had to be carried at once into the guest room in the office wing and put to bed. But on the threshold she turned around and spoke to them.

“It has been God’s storm,” she said, “God’s storm. I know now that everything has been for the best.”

With that, the door to the sickroom was closed, and they were not allowed to see her again.

Yet there is so much to say to someone who is dying. The words crowd upon one’s tongue when one knows that in the next room lies the one whose ear will soon be closed forever. “Ah, my friend, my friend,” one wishes to say, “can you forgive? Can you believe that I have loved you despite everything? How could it nevertheless come to pass that I should cause you so much sorrow while we walked here together? Ah, my friend, thank you for all the joy you have given me!”

This one wished to say, and so much, much else.

But the major’s wife lay in a burning fever, and the cavaliers’ voices could not reach her. Would she then never learn how they had worked, how they had taken up her work, how they had saved Ekeby’s honor and splendor? Would she never learn it?

Shortly afterward, the cavaliers went down to the smithy. All work there had stopped, but they threw fresh charcoal and fresh pig iron into the furnace and prepared a heat. They did not call the smiths, who had gone home to celebrate Christmas, but worked at the hearth themselves. If only the major’s wife could live until the hammer started up, then it would plead their case with her.

Evening came, and night came during the work. Several of them thought how strange it was that they had now once again come to celebrate Christmas night in the smithy.

The much-experienced Kevenhüller, who had been the master builder of the smithy and the mill during this busy time, and Kristian Bergh, the strong captain, stood by the hearth and tended the heat. Gösta and Julius hauled charcoal. Of the others, some sat on the anvil beneath the raised hammer, while others had settled down on charcoal carts and heaps of pig iron. Löwenborg, the old mystic, spoke with Uncle Eberbard, the philosopher, who sat beside him on the anvil.

“Tonight Sintram dies,” he said.

“Why tonight in particular?” Eberhard asked.

“Brother surely knows that last year we entered into a wager. Now we have done nothing that has not been worthy of cavaliers, and therefore he has lost.”

“Brother, who believes in such things, surely also knows that we have done much that has not been worthy of cavaliers. First, we did not help the major’s wife; second, we began to work; third, it was not entirely proper that Gösta Berling did not kill himself when he had promised to do so.”

“I have thought of this too,” Löwenborg said, “but I believe that Brother does not understand the matter correctly. We were forbidden to act with our own petty advantages in mind, but not to act as love or honor or our eternal salvation required. I believe that Sintram has lost.”

“Brother may be right.”

“I shall tell Brother that I know it. I have heard his sleigh bells all evening, but they are not real sleigh bells. Soon we shall have him here.”

And the little old man sat staring toward the smithy gate, which stood open, and toward the patch of blue sky studded with sparse stars that could be seen through it.

After a while, he started up.

“Does Brother see him?” he whispered. “There he comes now, slinking in. Does Brother not see him in the doorway?”

“I see nothing,” Uncle Eberhard replied. “Brother is sleepy; that is the whole matter.”

“I saw him so clearly against the bright sky. He was wearing his long wolfskin coat and fur cap. Now he is inside in the darkness, and I cannot see him. Look, now he is at the furnace! He is standing close beside Kristian Bergh, but Kristian evidently does not see him. Now he leans forward and throws something into the fire. Oh, how wicked he looks! Take care, friends, take care!”
